claim: DA9 is a bipolar excitatory motor neuron, the most posterior neuron of the DA class, with its cell body in the ventral midline.
source: DA9 is a bipolar excitatory motor neuron, the most posterior neuron of the DA class, with its cell body in the ventral midline.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electron microscopy reconstruction studies (Hall and Russell, 1991b; White et al., 1976; White et al., 1986).

claim: The DA9 dendrite extends anteriorly in the ventral nerve cord (VNC), receiving input from command neurons and sensory neurons.
source: According to the electron microscopy reconstruction, the DA9 dendrite extends anteriorly in the ventral nerve cord (VNC), receiving input from command neurons and sensory neurons (Hall and Russell, 1991b; White et al., 1976; White et al., 1986)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electron microscopy reconstruction studies.

claim: The DA9 axon extends posteriorly in the VNC and then crosses to the dorsal nerve cord (DNC) via a commissure.
source: The DA9 axon extends posteriorly in the VNC and then crosses to the dorsal nerve cord (DNC) via a commissure.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical description and citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: The DA9 axon proceeds anteriorly in the DNC and forms en passant cholinergic synapses that are dyadic with the posterior dorsal body wall muscles (BMWs) and the ventral D (VD) inhibitory GABA motor neurons.
source: It then proceeds anteriorly in the DNC and forms en passant cholinergic synapses that are dyadic with the posterior dorsal body wall muscles (BMWs) and the ventral D (VD) inhibitory GABA motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical description and citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: DA9 synapses are restricted to a small region of the DA9 axon.
source: These synapses are restricted to a small region of the DA9 axon, and the axon itself extends in the DNC past the synaptic region.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical description and citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: Based on its anatomy and connectivity, DA9 activity is predicted to trigger dorsal bending of the animal's tail region, by directly activating dorsal BMWs while simultaneously inhibiting opposing ventral BMWs via VD activity.
source: Based on its anatomy and connectivity, DA9 activity is predicted to trigger dorsal bending of the animal's tail region, by directly activating dorsal BMWs while simultaneously inhibiting opposing ventral BMWs via VD activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from anatomical connectivity data.

claim: 12 hr after axotomy, DA9 axons had initiated regeneration and regenerated past the injury site.
source: We found that 12 hr after axotomy, DA9 axons had initiated regeneration and regenerated past the injury site (Figure 1C), similar to the kinetics of regeneration in other neurons (Chuang et al., 2014; Hammarlund and Jin, 2014; Yanik et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1C and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Even after 12 hr, the distal axon fragment still was present.
source: However, even after 12 hr, the distal axon fragment still was present (Figure 1C), similar to slow removal of fragments after injury in other C. elegans neurons (Nichols et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1C and comparison to previous studies.

claim: DA9 develops normally in ric-7(n2657) animals compared to controls.
source: DA9 develops normally in ric-7(n2657) animals compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–1D), consistent with the previous data (Hao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–1D and citation to previous study.

claim: After laser axotomy of DA9, the distal axon segment degenerated quickly and was largely cleared away at 12 hr in ric-7(n2657) animals.
source: However, after laser axotomy of DA9, the distal axon segment degenerated quickly and was largely cleared away at 12 hr (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the GABA motor neuron system, ric-7(n2657) animals show enhanced degeneration together with increased regeneration 24 hr after axotomy.
source: In the GABA motor neuron system, ric-7(n2657) animals also show enhanced degeneration together with increased regeneration 24 hr after axotomy, indicating that loss of ric-7(n2657) and enhanced degeneration do not interfere with axon regeneration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–1H.

claim: Loss of ric-7(n2657) and enhanced degeneration do not interfere with axon regeneration.
source: In the GABA motor neuron system, ric-7(n2657) animals also show enhanced degeneration together with increased regeneration 24 hr after axotomy, indicating that loss of ric-7(n2657) and enhanced degeneration do not interfere with axon regeneration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–1H).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–1H.

claim: Axon growth occurred only in the first 48 hr after axotomy, after which no additional growth occurred.
source: Axon growth occurred only in the first 48 hr, after which no additional growth occurred (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: During regeneration, regenerating axons completely reinnervated their previous synaptic region, but failed to grow far past the synaptic region as observed before injury.
source: During this time, regenerating axons completely reinnervated their previous synaptic region, but failed to grow far past the synaptic region as observed before injury (Figure 2D and G; the grey stripe in Figure 2G indicates the synaptic region of regenerated axons 48 hr after axotomy).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and G.

claim: Lack of growth into the distal asynaptic area resulted in regenerated axons that only reach 1/3 of length of intact axons.
source: Lack of growth into the distal asynaptic area resulted in regenerated axons that only reach 1/3 of length of intact axons (Figure 2G, cut 72 hr vs uncut 48 hr, mean = 182.0 µm and 518.2 µm, p<0.0001, unpaired t test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 2G with statistical analysis.

claim: 100 percent (28/28) of severed DA9 axons initiated regeneration and reinnervated the synaptic region.
source: Overall, 100 percent (28/28) of severed DA9 axons initiated regeneration and reinnervated the synaptic region.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data.

claim: As DA9 regenerates, it forms new SV puncta coincident with regeneration.
source: As DA9 regenerates, it forms new SV puncta coincident with regeneration (Figure 2B–2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–2E.

claim: By 48 hr, when axon growth was completed, the number of SV puncta was statistically indistinguishable from intact animals and did not further increase.
source: By 48 hr, when axon growth was completed (Figure 2G), the number of SV puncta was statistically indistinguishable from intact animals and did not further increase (Figure 2E, cut 48 hr, cut 72 hr and uncut 48 hr, mean = 19.8, 19.3 and 20.2, p=0.7864, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 2E and G with statistical analysis.

claim: The new synapses were again localized in a specific region of the DNC.
source: The new synapses were again localized in a specific region of the DNC (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The position of the new synaptic region, as indicated by the length of the asynaptic region, was similar to intact animals.
source: The position of the new synaptic region, as indicated by the length of the asynaptic region (Figure 2A), was similar to intact animals (Figure 2F, uncut vs cut, mean = 31.8 µm and 36.7 µm, p=0.1238, unpaired t test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 2F with statistical analysis.

claim: The length of the synaptic region was shorter than in uninjured axons.
source: The largest difference was in the length of the synaptic region, which was shorter than in uninjured axons (Figure 2F, uncut vs cut, mean = 119.5 µm and 87.0 µm, p<0.0001, unpaired t test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 2F with statistical analysis.

claim: The regenerating DA9 axon is able to form new SV puncta and largely re-establish its synaptic pattern.
source: Overall, these data indicate that the regenerating DA9 axon is able to form new SV puncta and largely re-establish its synaptic pattern.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented.

claim: The process of axon regeneration, both in terms of axon regrowth and synapse reformation, ended by 48 hr after axotomy.
source: The process of axon regeneration, both in terms of axon regrowth and synapse reformation, ended by 48 hr after axotomy.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented.

claim: In intact animals, UNC-10 and CLA-1S puncta were predominantly localized to puncta in the DA9 synaptic region.
source: In intact animals, UNC-10 and CLA-1S puncta were predominantly localized to puncta in the DA9 synaptic region (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–2A'' and 2 C-2C'').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–2A'' and 2C-2C''.

claim: UNC-10 and CLA-1S puncta regenerated only partially in the new DA9 synaptic region 48 hr after axotomy.
source: However, unlike SVs, UNC-10 and CLA-1S puncta regenerated only partially in the new DA9 synaptic region 48 hr after axotomy (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–2B'' and 2D-2D'').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–2B'' and 2D-2D''.

claim: The number of UNC-10 and CLA-1S puncta after axotomy was about half the number in intact animals.
source: The number of UNC-10 and CLA-1S puncta after axotomy was about half the number in intact animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E and F.

claim: Some of the new SV clusters in the regenerated axons represent defective synapses.
source: These data suggest that some of the new SV clusters in the regenerated axons represent defective synapses, and indicate that mechanisms for regenerating SV clusters and active zones are at least partially distinct.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on UNC-10 and CLA-1S regeneration.

claim: Mechanisms for regenerating SV clusters and active zones are at least partially distinct.
source: These data suggest that some of the new SV clusters in the regenerated axons represent defective synapses, and indicate that mechanisms for regenerating SV clusters and active zones are at least partially distinct.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on differential regeneration of SV clusters versus active zone proteins.

claim: SV puncta also formed in the dendrite during regeneration.
source: Strikingly, SV puncta also formed in the dendrite during regeneration (Figure 2A–2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–2D.

claim: In intact animals, SV puncta were essentially absent from the dendrite.
source: In intact animals, SV puncta were essentially absent from the dendrite (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: After axon surgery, dendritic SVs became apparent at as early as 6 hr after axotomy.
source: After axon surgery, however, dendritic SVs became apparent at as early as 6 hr after axotomy (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The number of dendritic SV puncta reached a maximum at 12 hr (mean = 17.3) and decreased only slightly thereafter.
source: The number of puncta reached a maximum at 12 hr (mean = 17.3) and decreased only slightly thereafter.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data.

claim: The appearance of ectopic SVs in the dendrite was not caused by the ric-7(n2657) background, because control animals also accumulated a similar number of ectopic puncta in response to axotomy.
source: Importantly, the appearance of ectopic SVs in the dendrite was not caused by the ric-7(n2657) background, because control animals also accumulated a similar number of ectopic puncta in response to axotomy (Figure 2H, ric-7(n2657) cut 12 hr vs control cut 12 hr, mean = 17.3 and 16.6).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 2H comparing ric-7(n2657) and control animals.

claim: Axonal injury triggers ectopic accumulation of SVs in the dendrite, identifying an unexpected form of plasticity during recovery from nerve injury.
source: These data show that axonal injury triggers ectopic accumulation of SVs in the dendrite, identifying an unexpected form of plasticity during recovery from nerve injury.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on dendritic SV accumulation.

claim: In intact animals, both ACR-16::GFP and ACR-12::GFP puncta overlapped with the putative DA9 synaptic region.
source: In intact animals, both ACR-16::GFP and ACR-12::GFP puncta overlapped with the putative DA9 synaptic region (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–1A'').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–1A''.

claim: 48 hr after axotomy, the number of ACR-16 and ACR-12 puncta in the DA9 synaptic region was unchanged.
source: 48 hr after axotomy, the number of puncta in this region was unchanged (Figure 3B–3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–1C.

claim: The length of the region of the DA9 axon in the posterior dorsal nerve cord that is not apposed to ACR-12 or ACR-16 puncta was unchanged 48 hr after axotomy.
source: In addition, the length of the region of the DA9 axon in the posterior dorsal nerve cord that is not apposed to ACR-12 or ACR-16 puncta was also unchanged 48 hr after axotomy (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The number and localization of postsynaptic receptors to the DA9 synaptic region remain constant after injury and regeneration of the DA9 axon.
source: These data indicate that the number and localization of postsynaptic receptors to the DA9 synaptic region remain constant after injury and regeneration of the DA9 axon.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on postsynaptic receptor localization.

claim: In intact animals, about 90% of the BFP::RAB-3 puncta apposed or overlapped with ACR-12::GFP puncta.
source: In intact animals, about 90% of the BFP::RAB-3 puncta apposed or overlapped with ACR-12::GFP puncta (Figure 3E and G), consistent with the fact that DA9 normally forms dyadic synapses onto VD GABA neurons (as well as dorsal BWMs).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 3E and G and comparison to known anatomy.

claim: 48 hr after axotomy, 90% of the regenerated BFP::RAB-3 puncta in DA9 axon again apposed the ACR-12:GFP puncta.
source: 48 hr after axotomy, 90% of the regenerated BFP::RAB-3 puncta in DA9 axon again apposed the ACR-12:GFP puncta (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: The alignment of pre- and postsynaptic sites is restored after axotomy and regeneration to normal levels.
source: Therefore, the alignment of pre- and postsynaptic sites is restored after axotomy and regeneration to normal levels.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on pre- and postsynaptic alignment.

claim: In intact animals, ACR-16 puncta overlapped extensively with the DA9 dendrite.
source: In intact animals, ACR-16 puncta overlapped extensively with the DA9 dendrite (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–1A'').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–1A''.

claim: 48 hr after axotomy, the number of ACR-16 puncta juxtaposed to the DA9 dendrite was similar to uninjured animals.
source: 48 hr after axotomy, the number of ACR-16 puncta juxtaposed to the DA9 dendrite was similar to uninjured animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and E.

claim: The dendritic SV clusters that form in DA9 after axotomy do not induce significant numbers of new postsynaptic receptors in the ventral BWMs.
source: Thus, the dendritic SV clusters that form in DA9 after axotomy do not induce significant numbers of new postsynaptic receptors in the ventral BWMs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on ACR-16 localization.

claim: When 5 s of light stimulation was applied, freely behaving Chrimson-expressing animals displayed strong dorsal tail bending.
source: Indeed, when 5 s of light stimulation was applied, freely behaving Chrimson-expressing animals displayed strong dorsal tail bending (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Animals that expressed Chrimson and were cultured with all-trans-retinal (ATR) showed an average of 80 degrees of dorsal bending, time-locked to the light stimulus.
source: Animals that expressed Chrimson and were cultured with all-trans-retinal (ATR) showed an average of 80 degrees of dorsal bending, time-locked to the light stimulus (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Dorsal bending in response to light was observed in every animal (N = 42).
source: Dorsal bending in response to light was observed in every animal (N = 42).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data.

claim: Animals that did not express Chrimson or that were not given ATR, showed no response to light stimulation.
source: Animals that did not express Chrimson or that were not given ATR, showed no response to light stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B and D.

claim: The behavior of Chrimson-expressing animals cultured with ATR was abolished 12 hr after DA9 cell body was ablated by laser.
source: In addition, the behavior of Chrimson-expressing animals cultured with ATR was abolished 12 hr after DA9 cell body was ablated by laser (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: 5 min after axotomy of DA9, light activation of DA9 did not cause dorsal bending behavior.
source: 5 min after axotomy of DA9, light activation of DA9 did not cause dorsal bending behavior (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Axotomy proximal to the known DA9 synaptic region completely disconnects DA9 from its outputs.
source: These data confirmed that the bending behavior was specifically driven by DA9, and indicate that axotomy proximal to the known DA9 synaptic region completely disconnects DA9 from its outputs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on behavior after axotomy.

claim: Chrimson-mediated neuronal output in DA9 requires connection to the cell body.
source: Thus, Chrimson-mediated neuronal output in DA9 requires connection to the cell body.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that the distal fragment containing Chrimson was insufficient to trigger tail bending.

claim: 48 hr after axon injury, when axon and synapse regeneration was complete, behavior had partially recovered.
source: 48 hr after axon injury, when axon and synapse regeneration was complete (Figure 2E and G), we found that behavior had partially recovered (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, G and Figure 4G.

claim: At 72 hr, consistent with the lack of further morphological growth after 48 hr, there was no further behavioral recovery.
source: At 72 hr, consistent with the lack of further morphological growth after 48 hr, there was no further behavioral recovery (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H and comparison to morphological data.

claim: The maximum behavioral recovery was on average about 1/3 of the control animals.
source: Thus, the maximum behavioral recovery was on average about 1/3 of the control animals (Figure 4I, cut 72 hr vs control, mean = 26.3° and 70.5°, p<0.0001, unpaired t test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 4I with statistical analysis.

claim: Recovered behavior after injury was far more variable than behavior in intact animals.
source: A major reason for limited recovery on average was that recovered behavior after injury was far more variable than behavior in intact animals: while more than half of injured animals recovered dorsal bending, many did not.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on behavioral recovery.

claim: At least some of the newly formed SV puncta in the axon are functional regenerated synapses.
source: Nevertheless, these data indicate that at least some of the newly formed SV puncta in the axon are functional regenerated synapses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on behavioral recovery.

claim: Recovered dorsal bending was completely abolished after recutting DA9 in animals that displayed behavioral recovery at 48 hr.
source: Recovered dorsal bending was completely abolished after recutting, indicating that behavioral recovery was due to DA9 regeneration (Figure 4J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J and K.

claim: Behavioral recovery was due to DA9 regeneration.
source: Recovered dorsal bending was completely abolished after recutting, indicating that behavioral recovery was due to DA9 regeneration (Figure 4J and K).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on recutting.

claim: No behavioral responses were detected in either intact or axotomized unc-13(e51) animals 48 hr after axotomy.
source: We detected no behavioral responses in either intact or axotomized animals 48 hr after axotomy (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The tail-bending behavior is mediated by chemical synapses in both intact and regenerated animals.
source: This suggests that the tail-bending behavior is mediated by chemical synapses in both intact and regenerated animals.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data in unc-13(e51) animals.

claim: At 12 hr after axotomy, on average, DA9 activation resulted in ventral rather than dorsal bending.
source: At 12 hr after axotomy, we found that on average, DA9 activation resulted in ventral rather than dorsal bending (Figure 4E and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and I.

claim: At 12 hr, more than half of the animals bent their tail ventrally, rather than dorsally.
source: Data from individual animals revealed that at 12 hr, more than half of the animals bent their tail ventrally, rather than dorsally.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from individual animals.

claim: DA9 activation in regenerated neurons was causing behavior opposite to uninjured neurons.
source: Thus, DA9 activation in these regenerated neurons was causing behavior opposite to uninjured neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on ventral bending.

claim: Even at 48 and 72 hr after injury some animals still exhibited ventral bending.
source: This aberrant behavior was observed less frequently as regeneration proceeds, but even at 48 and 72 hr after injury some animals still exhibited ventral bending (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Although injury and regeneration can restore normal behavior in some individuals, in other individuals injury and regeneration result in formation of a pathological circuit that drives novel and inappropriate behavior.
source: These data demonstrate that although injury and regeneration can restore normal behavior in some individuals, in other individuals injury and regeneration result in formation of a pathological circuit that drives novel and inappropriate behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on behavioral variability.

claim: In intact animals, dorsal BWMs displayed robust increases in Ca2+ levels during light stimulation of DA9.
source: In intact animals, we found that dorsal BWMs displayed robust increases in Ca2+ levels during light stimulation of DA9, consistent with DA9 directly activating these muscles (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: In intact animals, simultaneous decreases in ventral BWM Ca2+ levels were observed, presumably mediated by DA9 activation of inhibitory GABAergic VD motor neurons.
source: We also observed simultaneous decreases in ventral BWM Ca2+ levels, presumably mediated by DA9 activation of inhibitory GABAergic VD motor neurons as predicted by the wiring diagram (Figure 5F and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and J and inference from the wiring diagram.

claim: Animals cultured without ATR displayed no Ca2+ changes at all during stimulation.
source: Importantly, animals cultured without ATR displayed no Ca2+ changes at all during stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating that all the calcium transients are specifically due to activation of Chrimson in DA9.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All the calcium transients are specifically due to activation of Chrimson in DA9.
source: Importantly, animals cultured without ATR displayed no Ca2+ changes at all during stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating that all the calcium transients are specifically due to activation of Chrimson in DA9.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data in animals without ATR.

claim: 12 hr after axotomy, dorsal BWMs showed little Ca2+ increase in response to light stimulation.
source: In sharp contrast to the results in uninjured animals, we found that 12 hr after axotomy, dorsal BWMs showed little Ca2+ increase in response to light stimulation (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and E.

claim: The maximum Ca2+ amplitude in dorsal BWMs 12 hr after axotomy was about 12% of the control animals.
source: The maximum Ca2+ amplitude in dorsal BWMs 12 hr after axotomy was about 12% of the control animals (Figure 5G, mean = 0.23 and 1.84 with and without axotomy).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: DA9 activation 12 hr after axotomy drove strong Ca2+ increases in ventral BWMs.
source: Further, DA9 activation 12 hr after axotomy drove strong Ca2+ increases in ventral BWMs, consistent with the dendritic SV localization and the ventral bending behavior at the 12 hr time point (Figure 5F and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and H.

claim: 48 hr after axotomy, DA9 activation was more effective at driving dorsal BWMs, which displayed Ca2+ increases about 35% of the controls.
source: 48 hr after axotomy, DA9 activation was more effective at driving dorsal BWMs, which displayed Ca2+ increases about 35% of the controls, confirming that new synapses in the axon are functional (Figure 5D, J and K; mean = 0.32 and 0.91 with and without axotomy in Figure 5K).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 5D, J and K.

claim: New synapses in the axon are functional.
source: 48 hr after axotomy, DA9 activation was more effective at driving dorsal BWMs, which displayed Ca2+ increases about 35% of the controls, confirming that new synapses in the axon are functional (Figure 5D, J and K; mean = 0.32 and 0.91 with and without axotomy in Figure 5K).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on Ca2+ responses in dorsal BWMs.

claim: Even at the 48 hr time point, the ventral BWMs also displayed Ca2+ increases, suggesting that the ectopic synapses in the dendrite are still functional at 48 hr after axotomy.
source: Even at the 48 hr time point, however, the ventral BWMs also displayed Ca2+ increases, suggesting that the ectopic synapses in the dendrite are still functional at 48 hr after axotomy (Figure 5J and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J and L and inference about dendritic synapse function.

claim: Information transfer—the fundamental role of neurons—is rerouted after axon injury and regeneration.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that information transfer—the fundamental role of neurons—is rerouted after axon injury and regeneration.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on Ca2+ responses in muscles.

claim: No Ca2+ signals were detected in either intact or axotomized unc-13(e51) animals 48 hr after axotomy.
source: No Ca2+ signals were detected in either intact or axotomized animals 48 hr after axotomy (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Postsynaptic calcium responses due to DA9 stimulation are mediated by chemical synapses in both intact and regenerated axons.
source: These data indicate that postsynaptic calcium responses due to DA9 stimulation are mediated by chemical synapses in both intact and regenerated axons, consistent with the results from behavioral analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data in unc-13(e51) animals and comparison to behavioral data.

claim: DA9 axons completely failed to regenerate in ric-7(n2657); dlk-1(ju476) animals.
source: Consistent with these previous results, we found that DA9 axons completely failed to regenerate in ric-7(n2657); dlk-1(ju476) animals (Figure 6A–6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–6C and comparison to previous studies.

claim: dlk-1(ju476) mutant animals still mislocalized SV puncta ectopically to the dendrite after axotomy, at similar levels as controls.
source: Despite this lack of axonal response, however, dlk-1(ju476) mutant animals still mislocalized SV puncta ectopically to the dendrite after axotomy, at similar levels as controls (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: Mislocalization of SVs to the dendrite in response to injury is independent of dlk-1 function.
source: Together these data indicate that ectopic synapses in the DA9 dendrite can mediate ventral bending even at 48 hr after axotomy. These data also indicate that mislocalization of SVs to the dendrite in response to injury is independent of dlk-1 function.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data in dlk-1(ju476) mutant animals.

claim: Loss of dlk-1 had no detectable effect on the morphology or function of DA9 in the absence of injury.
source: Loss of dlk-1 had no detectable effect on the morphology (Figure 6A) or function of DA9; in the absence of injury, dlk-1(ju476) mutant animals showed robust dorsal bending of the tail (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: When DA9 was activated in dlk-1(ju476) mutant animals 12 or 48 hr after axotomy, almost all animals bent their tail ventrally.
source: However, when DA9 was activated in dlk-1(ju476) mutant animals 12 or 48 hr after axotomy, almost all animals bent their tail ventrally (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–1D.

claim: Ectopic synapses in the DA9 dendrite can mediate ventral bending even at 48 hr after axotomy.
source: Together these data indicate that ectopic synapses in the DA9 dendrite can mediate ventral bending even at 48 hr after axotomy.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data in dlk-1(ju476) mutant animals.

claim: Removing the dendrite increased dorsal bending about twofold 48 hr after axotomy.
source: We found that removing the dendrite increased dorsal bending about twofold (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: Even after regeneration is complete, misdirected SV release from the dendrite suppresses behavioral recovery.
source: This result indicates that even after regeneration is complete, misdirected SV release from the dendrite suppresses behavioral recovery.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on dendrite removal.

claim: Even after dendrite removal, DA9-driven behavior still did not reach the level observed in uninjured controls.
source: However, even after dendrite removal, DA9-driven behavior still did not reach the level observed in uninjured controls (Figure 6G, 48 hr recovery, recovery +dendrite cut and no cut control, mean = 20.0°, 38.2° and 77.4°, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Axonal activity is only able to drive behavior to about 50% of pre-injury levels even when dendritic suppression is removed.
source: Thus, axonal activity is only able to drive behavior to about 50% of pre-injury levels even when dendritic suppression is removed.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the quantitative experimental data on behavior after dendrite removal.

claim: Functional deficits in regenerated synapses are consistent with the molecular deficits observed in regenerated synapses, where many regenerated synapses have undetectable levels of the active zone components UNC-10 and CLA-1S.
source: These functional deficits in regenerated synapses are consistent with the molecular deficits we observed in regenerated synapses, where many regenerated synapses have undetectable levels of the active zone components UNC-10 and CLA-1S (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on active zone proteins and behavioral recovery.

claim: The failure of regeneration to restore particular molecular components to synapses results in persistent functional deficits.
source: These data suggest that the failure of regeneration to restore particular molecular components to synapses results in persistent functional deficits.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on molecular and functional deficits.

claim: In uninjured DA9 neurons, MT polarity in the axon was nearly completely plus-end out, while MT polarity in the dendrite was dominated by plus-end in MTs.
source: We found that in uninjured DA9 neurons, MT polarity in the axon was nearly completely plus-end out, while MT polarity in the dendrite was dominated by plus-end in MTs, consistent with previous results (Maniar et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2013) (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Axon injury did not result in polarity reversal in the axon or dendrite.
source: Surprisingly, however, axon injury did not result in polarity reversal in the axon or dendrite; in fact, in the dendrite after axon injury plus-end in MTs were even more dominant than before injury (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Axotomy had a significant effect on MT dynamics in both axons and dendrites, with an increased number of EBP-2 traces observed in both compartments.
source: Although axotomy did not reverse the polarity of MTs, it did have a significant effect on MT dynamics in both axons and dendrites. In both compartments, we observed an increased number of EBP-2 traces (Figure 7G), which has also been observed in C. elegans mechanosensory neurons (Chuang et al., 2014; Ghosh-Roy et al., 2012) and Drosophila sensory neurons (Stone et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Neuronal injury in DA9 results in increased MT dynamics but no change in MT polarity.
source: Overall, neuronal injury in DA9 results in increased MT dynamics but no change in MT polarity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on MT polarity and dynamics.

claim: Dendritic SV mislocalization is not a consequence of MT polarity changes.
source: Thus, dendritic SV mislocalization is not a consequence of MT polarity changes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on MT polarity.

claim: In uninjured DA9 neurons, ACR-2::GFP was highly enriched in the dendrite and soma and was absent from the axon.
source: We found that in uninjured DA9 neurons, ACR-2::GFP was highly enriched in the dendrite and soma and was absent from the axon (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), as previously described (Barbagallo et al., 2010; Qi et al., 2013; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and comparison to previous studies.

claim: 12 hr after injury, when ectopic SVs are highly enriched in the dendrite, localization of ACR-2::GFP was not different from uninjured neurons.
source: 12 hr after injury, when ectopic SVs are highly enriched in the dendrite (Figure 2H), localization of ACR-2::GFP was not different from uninjured neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and comparison to Figure 2H.

claim: Axon injury does not globally push the DA9 dendrite toward becoming axon-like.
source: Together, these results indicate that axon injury does not globally push the DA9 dendrite toward becoming axon-like, and suggest that more specific cellular mechanisms must mediate ectopic SV localization.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on MT polarity and ACR-2 localization.

claim: More specific cellular mechanisms must mediate ectopic SV localization.
source: Together, these results indicate that axon injury does not globally push the DA9 dendrite toward becoming axon-like, and suggest that more specific cellular mechanisms must mediate ectopic SV localization.
evidence: This claim is based on inference and speculation from the experimental data.

claim: dhc-1(js319) mutants had largely normal SV distribution in DA9 prior to injury.
source: These mutants had largely normal SV distribution in DA9 prior to injury (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The dhc-1(js319) mutation completely suppressed the dendritic accumulation of SVs at 48 hr after axotomy.
source: However, after injury we found that the dhc-1(js319) mutation completely suppressed the dendritic accumulation of SVs at 48 hr after axotomy (Figure 8B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and E.

claim: Partial suppression of dendritic SV accumulation was obtained in animals mutant for nud-2(ok949).
source: Partial suppression was obtained in animals mutant for another component of the dynein complex, nud-2(ok949), which is the worm ortholog of Nudel (Figure 8C and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C and E.

claim: Dynein-mediated transport is required for SV mislocalization in the dendrite in response to axotomy.
source: Together these data indicate that dynein-mediated transport is required for SV mislocalization in the dendrite in response to axotomy.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data in dynein mutants.

claim: JNK-1 is required for ectopic synapse formation in the dendrite after axotomy.
source: Here, we found that JNK-1 is required for ectopic synapse formation in the dendrite after axotomy (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: jnk-1(gk7) mutant animals showed very few SV puncta in the dendrite 48 hr and 12 hr after axotomy.
source: By contrast, after axon injury jnk-1(gk7) mutant animals showed very few SV puncta in the dendrite 48 hr (Figure 8D and E) and 12 hr after axotomy (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D, E and Figure 8—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: Ectopic synapse formation in the dendrite after axon injury requires the JNK3 homolog jnk-1.
source: Thus, ectopic synapse formation in the dendrite after axon injury requires the JNK3 homolog jnk-1.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data in jnk-1 mutants.

claim: Without axon injury, jnk-1(gk7) mutants showed robust dorsal bending in response to light stimulation, although the degree of dorsal bending was smaller compared to controls.
source: Without axon injury, jnk-1(gk7) mutants showed robust dorsal bending in response to light stimulation, although the degree of dorsal bending was smaller compared to controls (Figure 8F and G, jnk-1(gk7); ric-7(n2657) intact vs ric-7(n2657) intact, mean = 59.7° and 70.1°, p=0.0003, unpaired t test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 8F and G with statistical analysis.

claim: 48 hr after axotomy, the jnk-1(gk7) mutants showed improved dorsal bending behavior compared to controls.
source: By contrast, 48 hr after axotomy, the jnk-1(gk7) mutants showed improved dorsal bending behavior compared to controls (Figure 8F and G), similar to the improved behavior seen after dendrite removal (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F and G and comparison to dendrite removal experiments.

claim: Altering neuronal cellular mechanisms to correctly direct information transfer in regenerated circuits improves behavioral recovery after nerve injury.
source: Thus, altering neuronal cellular mechanisms to correctly direct information transfer in regenerated circuits improves behavioral recovery after nerve injury.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data in jnk-1 mutants and dendrite removal experiments.

claim: Severing DA9 close to the dorsal nerve cord allows regeneration across the former synaptic area to occur in essentially all animals studied.
source: We find that severing DA9 close to the dorsal nerve cord allows regeneration across the former synaptic area to occur in essentially all animals studied.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on DA9 regeneration.

claim: By using the ric-7(n2657) genetic background to promote removal of the distal axon fragment, regenerative growth in DA9 occurs without confounding issues of axonal fusion or other potential effects of the remaining fragment.
source: Further, by using the ric-7(n2657) genetic background to promote removal of the distal axon fragment, regenerative growth in DA9 occurs without confounding issues of axonal fusion or other potential effects of the remaining fragment.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on ric-7(n2657) animals.

claim: In the ric-7(n2657) background, functional recovery can occur only if new, functional synapses are rebuilt onto relevant targets.
source: In this work, by using the ric-7(n2657) background to promote distal segment removal, functional recovery can occur only if new, functional synapses are rebuilt onto relevant targets.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental design using ric-7(n2657) animals.

claim: The approach in DA9 in the ric-7(n2657) background allows for the first time detailed morphological analysis of synapse reformation in a single neuron during axon regeneration.
source: In combination, our approach in DA9 in the ric-7(n2657) background allows for the first time detailed morphological analysis of synapse reformation in a single neuron during axon regeneration.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental approach described.

claim: By applying the modern neuroscience tools of calcium imaging and optogenetics to DA9 and its target muscles, it is possible to analyze the function of this single neuron in its endogenous circuit and also with respect to its ability to drive behavior.
source: Further, by applying the modern neuroscience tools of calcium imaging and optogenetics to DA9 and its target muscles, it is possible to analyze the function of this single neuron in its endogenous circuit and also with respect to its ability to drive behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental approach described.

claim: DA9 axons do regenerate and form functional synapses in the correct location after axotomy.
source: We show that DA9 axons do regenerate and form functional synapses in the correct location after axotomy.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented throughout the study.

claim: Synapses also form ectopically in the dendrite, resulting in aberrant information routing and limiting behavioral recovery.
source: However, we find that synapses also form ectopically in the dendrite, resulting in aberrant information routing and limiting behavioral recovery.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented throughout the study.

claim: Ectopic synapse formation is reminiscent of the transformation of a dendrite to an axon after axon removal, but is a fundamentally different process.
source: Although ectopic synapse formation is reminiscent of the transformation of a dendrite to an axon after axon removal (Cho and So, 1992; Dotti and Banker, 1987; Fenrich et al., 2007; Gomis-Rüth et al., 2008; Hall et al., 1989; Hoang et al., 2005; Stone et al., 2010), we found that it is a fundamentally different process.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Dendrite-axon transformation requires axon removal, while in the DA9 experiments the axon is severed distant from the cell body, regenerates, and reforms functional synapses.
source: First, dendrite-axon transformation requires axon removal, while in our experiments the axon is severed distant from the cell body, regenerates, and reforms functional synapses.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the experimental data to previous studies on dendrite-axon transformation.

claim: Dendrite-axon transformation is accompanied by a rearrangement of MT polarity from dendritic orientation to axonal orientation.
source: Second, dendrite-axon transformation is accompanied by a rearrangement of MT polarity from dendritic orientation to axonal orientation (Stone et al., 2010; Takahashi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the case of DA9, dendritic microtubule polarity as well as nAChR localization is maintained after axotomy.
source: In the case of DA9, however, dendritic microtubule polarity as well as nAChR localization is maintained after axotomy (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The results define a novel cell-biological response to nerve injury.
source: Thus, our results define a novel cell-biological response to nerve injury.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing ectopic synapse formation without dendrite-axon transformation.
